## From a column to fluxes: what pyharp computes (`Radiation`, `RadiationBand`) {#sec-ch01-pipeline}

### Summary

pyharp computes the radiative fluxes of a column of atmosphere: the upward and downward energy per unit area and
time that sunlight and thermal emission carry through each level. The caller gives the species concentrations and
the layer thicknesses of one or many columns, and the level temperatures where the column emits. For each spectral
band of its configuration, pyharp asks the band's opacity modules for optical properties, combines them into the
optical depth, single-scattering albedo and phase-function moments of each layer, hands these to a radiative-transfer
solver, and sums the solver's fluxes over the spectral points of the band; it then sums the bands and returns the net
flux at every level, the downward flux at the surface and the upward flux at the top.

::: {.callout-note title="At a glance"}
**Purpose.** Column fluxes from concentrations: @eq-ch01-pipeline-prop, @eq-ch01-pipeline-band, @eq-ch01-pipeline-net.

**Data.** Concentration [$\mathrm{mol\,m^{-3}}$] (columns, layers, species), $\Delta z$ [m], level temperatures [K].

**Placement.** `Radiation.forward`, which runs `RadiationBand.forward` for each band in turn.

**Activation.** A YAML file read by `RadiationOptions.from_yaml`; spectral weights or wavenumbers set in Python.

**Guarantee / limits.** The sums are exact; the accuracy is that of the opacities and the solver.

**Evidence.** See the Tests layer.
:::

Local symbols: $a$, index of an opacity module of a band; $k_a$, extinction coefficient it returns
[$\mathrm{m^{-1}}$]; $\omega_a$, its single-scattering albedo [-]; $\chi_{a,n}$, its phase-function moment $n$ [-];
$\Delta z$, layer thickness [m]; $j$, index of a spectral point of a band; $w_j$, its weight [-]; $\nu_j$, its
wavenumber [$\mathrm{cm^{-1}}$]; $b$, index of a band; $F^{\uparrow}$, $F^{\downarrow}$, upward and downward flux at
a level as the solvers return them, the downward one including the direct beam [$\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$];
$F_{\mathrm{net}} = F^{\uparrow} - F^{\downarrow}$ [$\mathrm{W\,m^{-2}}$].

Of pydisort, kintera and snapy, pyharp depends only on pydisort, which provides the DISORT solver (`pydisort>=1.7.1`
in {{< code pyproject.toml repo=pyharp >}}, which also lists pyharp's other Python dependencies); the Toon solver is
part of pyharp. kintera and snapy are not dependencies. The example `run_sub_neptune_rt.py` shows how the three meet:
snapy holds the atmosphere's state on its mesh, kintera turns temperature, pressure and mole fractions into the
concentrations pyharp needs, and pyharp's net flux becomes a heating rate that the example adds to snapy's energy
equation (`_compute_rt_heating`, {{< code examples/run_sub_neptune_rt.py _compute_rt_heating repo=pyharp >}}).

### Derivation

**Step 1: the solver input of a band.** Each opacity module $a$ of a band returns, for each spectral point, column
and layer, an extinction coefficient $k_a$, a single-scattering albedo $\omega_a$ and phase-function moments
$\chi_{a,n}$ (@sec-ch02-delta-scaling defines the moments). Extinction adds; the albedo is the scattering-weighted
mean, and each moment is the mean over the scattered light:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Delta\tau &= \Delta z \sum_a k_a , \\
\omega &= \frac{\sum_a \omega_a k_a}{\sum_a k_a} , \\
\chi_n &= \frac{\sum_a \chi_{a,n}\,\omega_a k_a}{\sum_a \omega_a k_a} .
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch01-pipeline-prop}
<!-- equation-check: eq-ch01-pipeline-prop check_ch01_quickstart.py [C2] -->

@eq-ch01-pipeline-prop is computed in `RadiationBandImpl::forward`
({{< code src/radiation/radiation_band.cpp RadiationBandImpl::forward repo=pyharp >}}), which sums
$\omega_a k_a$ and $\chi_{a,n}\omega_a k_a$ first and divides through `divide_where_positive`, so a layer with no
extinction gets $\omega = 0$ and a layer with no scattering gets $\chi_n = 0$. When the band's optical properties include
an albedo channel (`nprop > 1`), the same function then replaces $\omega$ by $\min(\omega, 1 - \delta\omega)$, with
$\delta\omega = 10^{-12}$ in double precision and $10^{-6}$ otherwise, before the solver runs (@sec-ch02-conservation).

**Step 2: the flux of a band.** The solver returns $F^{\uparrow}_j$ and $F^{\downarrow}_j$ at every level for each
spectral point $j$. A band either has weights $w_j$ (for example the weights of a correlated-k quadrature) or a
wavenumber grid $\nu_j$, and its flux is the weighted sum or the trapezoid rule:

$$
\begin{aligned}
F_b &= \sum_j w_j F_j , \\
F_b &= \sum_j \tfrac12\left(\nu_{j+1} - \nu_j\right)\left(F_j + F_{j+1}\right) ,
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch01-pipeline-band}
<!-- equation-check: eq-ch01-pipeline-band check_ch01_quickstart.py [C4] -->
<!-- equation-check: eq-ch01-pipeline-band check_ch01_quickstart.py [C5] -->

for $F$ either $F^{\uparrow}$ or $F^{\downarrow}$. @eq-ch01-pipeline-band is computed in `sum_spectrum`
({{< code src/radiation/flux_utils.cpp sum_spectrum repo=pyharp >}}), called by `RadiationBandImpl::forward`; the
first line is used when the band has weights, the second otherwise.

**Step 3: the column outputs.** The bands are summed level by level, and the net flux follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}
F^{\uparrow} &= \sum_b F^{\uparrow}_b , \\
F^{\downarrow} &= \sum_b F^{\downarrow}_b , \\
F_{\mathrm{net}} &= F^{\uparrow} - F^{\downarrow} \quad \text{at every level}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-ch01-pipeline-net}
<!-- equation-check: eq-ch01-pipeline-net check_ch01_quickstart.py [C3] -->

Three quantities are returned: $F_{\mathrm{net}}$ at every level, $F^{\downarrow}$ at the surface and $F^{\uparrow}$
at the top.

@eq-ch01-pipeline-net is computed in `RadiationImpl::forward`
({{< code src/radiation/radiation.cpp RadiationImpl::forward repo=pyharp >}}) with `cal_net_flux`,
`cal_surface_flux` and `cal_toa_flux` ({{< code src/radiation/flux_utils.cpp cal_net_flux repo=pyharp >}},
{{< code src/radiation/flux_utils.cpp cal_surface_flux repo=pyharp >}},
{{< code src/radiation/flux_utils.cpp cal_toa_flux repo=pyharp >}}). $F_{\mathrm{net}}$ is positive where more
energy goes up than down. Steps 1 to 3 are sums and quotients with no approximation; the approximations of a flux
calculation are in the opacities and in the solver, documented in @sec-ch03, @sec-ch04 and @sec-ch05. The executable
check is `check_ch01_quickstart.py`.

### Numerical method

Every quantity of a band is a tensor with the spectral points first and the columns second, so one call handles
all columns and spectral points at once; @fig-ch01-pipeline-shapes gives the shapes. Layer quantities are indexed
from the surface (layer 0) to the top, and level quantities from the surface (level 0) to the top (level $n_{\mathrm{lyr}}$,
the number of layers). The Toon solver returns four channels per level (upward, downward, and the two at the midpoint
of the layer below); DISORT returns two, and `RadiationBandImpl::forward` copies them into the midpoint channels so
that bands of both solvers can be summed.

```{python}
#| label: fig-ch01-pipeline-shapes
#| fig-cap: "Where the quantities of one band live. Left: a column of four layers (light blue) and its five levels (orange ticks), numbered from the surface. Right: the shape of each tensor along the pipeline; nwave is the number of spectral points, ncol of columns, nlyr of layers, nlev = nlyr + 1 of levels, nprop of optical properties. Layer quantities are light blue, level quantities orange."
#| fig-alt: "A stack of four boxes labelled layer 0 at the bottom to layer 3 at the top, with level 0 (surface) to level 4 (top) at their boundaries. Beside it, five rows: opacity output and solver input prop with shape nwave, ncol, nlyr, nprop; solver output spectrum with shape nwave, ncol, nlev, 2 or 4; band flux ncol, nlev, 4; Radiation.forward returns ncol by nlev, then ncol and ncol."
#| echo: false
from pyharp_report.ch01.figures.fig_pipeline_shapes import make_fig
```

### Code

| what | code link | symbol | switch |
|---|---|---|---|
| column | {{< code src/radiation/radiation.cpp RadiationImpl::forward repo=pyharp >}} | `bands`, `spectra` | always |
| band | {{< code src/radiation/radiation_band.cpp RadiationBandImpl::forward repo=pyharp >}} | `prop`, `spectrum` | always |
| solver choice | {{< code src/radiation/radiation_band.cpp RadiationBandImpl::reset repo=pyharp >}} | `rtsolver` | `solver` |
| band sum | {{< code src/radiation/flux_utils.cpp sum_spectrum repo=pyharp >}} | `weight`, `wavenumber` | which is set |
| pydisort dependency | {{< code pyproject.toml repo=pyharp >}} | `pydisort>=1.7.1` | always |

: Code map of the pipeline. {#tbl-ch01-pipeline-code}

1. `RadiationImpl::forward` calls `forward` of each band in the order of the configuration and stacks their
   results in the buffer `spectra` ({{< code src/radiation/radiation.cpp RadiationImpl::forward repo=pyharp >}}).
2. `RadiationBandImpl::forward` calls each opacity module with the concentrations and the band's keyword inputs,
   accumulates @eq-ch01-pipeline-prop in the buffer `prop`, multiplies by $\Delta z$, caps $\omega$, and calls the
   solver ({{< code src/radiation/radiation_band.cpp RadiationBandImpl::forward repo=pyharp >}}).
3. `RadiationBandImpl::reset` creates the solver named by the band's `solver` key, `disort` or `toon`, and refuses a
   band with neither weights nor wavenumbers
   ({{< code src/radiation/radiation_band.cpp RadiationBandImpl::reset repo=pyharp >}}).
4. `sum_spectrum` applies @eq-ch01-pipeline-band ({{< code src/radiation/flux_utils.cpp sum_spectrum repo=pyharp >}}).
5. `RadiationImpl::forward` sums the bands and returns @eq-ch01-pipeline-net; when the atmosphere input carries
   `area`, it also scales the fluxes for a spherical shell (answered at @sec-ch08-spherical).

### Tests

| test (ctest name) | what it asserts | tolerance | where the tolerance comes from |
|---|---|---|---|
| `check_ch01_quickstart.py` `[C2]` | @eq-ch01-pipeline-prop for a gas and a haze | $10^{-15}$ relative | two products and a quotient |
| `check_ch01_quickstart.py` `[C3]` | @eq-ch01-pipeline-net from the `spectra` buffer | $10^{-14}$ of the largest band flux | one sum, one difference |
| `check_ch01_quickstart.py` `[C4]` | @eq-ch01-pipeline-band, weights $(0.25, 0.75)$ | $10^{-15}$ relative | one weighted sum |
| `check_ch01_quickstart.py` `[C5]` | @eq-ch01-pipeline-band, three wavenumbers | $10^{-15}$ relative | the trapezoid rule |

: Tests of the pipeline. {#tbl-ch01-pipeline-tests}

`[C2]` reads the solver input of the quick start's shortwave band, a gas with $\omega_a = 0$ and $k_a\Delta z = 0.75$
per layer and a haze with $\omega_a = 1$, $\chi_{a,1} = 0.6$ and $k_a\Delta z = 0.25$. It runs the two compiled
opacities itself, computes @eq-ch01-pipeline-prop from their outputs, and finds $\Delta\tau = 1$, $\omega = 0.25$ and
$\chi_1 = 0.6$ in the band. Because the two extinctions differ, the case separates the weighted mean from the plain
mean of the albedos ($0.5$) and from the mean with the two weights exchanged ($0.75$); the check requires both to be
more than $0.1$ away, so a mixing rule that drops or swaps the weights fails it: with pyharp rebuilt to use the plain
mean, or the complement of the weighted mean, `[C2]` fails on both pydisort pins and the unchanged build passes
(`ch01_breaks.sh`). `[C4]` and `[C5]` use a band whose spectral points have different optical depths, so their fluxes
differ and the weights matter. All pass on both pydisort pins with the same lines[^ch01-pipeline-run]. The solvers
themselves are tested in @sec-ch03, @sec-ch04 and @sec-ch05; pyharp's own tests are listed in @sec-ch10-test-suite.

### Limits

- **One precision per call.** The band's buffers are double precision unless the module is moved to another type;
  single precision is answered at @sec-ch09-toon.
- **Spherical scaling.** The scaling applied when `area` is given: answered at @sec-ch08-spherical.
- **Opacity types.** The opacity modules a band can use are the types `RadiationBandImpl::reset` creates; their
  physics: not provided: it belongs to the opacity chapter, not to this overview.
